passage: Teacher's note, Grade 6 spelling test. Baljeet leaned across the aisle and whispered to Lokesh, "Let me see what you wrote, Lokesh. We're friends, aren't we?" I was two desks away and heard it. Lokesh's ears went red and he moved his arm over his sheet. "I can't. We'll both get into trouble," he said, barely audible. Baljeet sat back in his chair with a scowl. At recess I saw them on the bench, Lokesh holding the word list and testing Baljeet on the tricky ones. Later Lokesh told me he had hated that moment because he did not want to lose his friend. I did not need to step in, and I told him so.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh and Baljeet sit at recess?
qa.a: They sat on the bench, with Lokesh holding the word list.

qa.q: What was Lokesh worried about when he refused?
qa.a: He was worried about both of them getting into trouble, and about losing his friend; he told the teacher he hated that moment because he did not want to lose his friend.

qa.q: What would you advise Lokesh if Baljeet asks again?
qa.a: He can keep saying no kindly and repeat his offer to practise the words together, since a real friend would not want him to risk trouble.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when Lokesh refused?
qa.a: Baljeet may have felt embarrassed or annoyed, as the scowl suggests, yet still sat with Lokesh at recess, so he may also have been glad of the help.

grounding: Illustrates a child pressed by a friend to share answers, feeling torn, refusing and offering to help him study.

passage:
Thursday. Mridul caught Nikita at the gate. 'Tomorrow's Hindi test. Just tilt your paper a bit, okay? We're friends, after all.' Nikita laughed nervously and didn't answer.
Friday. In the test, Mridul coughed twice, the signal he had suggested. Nikita felt her face burn. She wanted to help him; they had been friends since nursery. But her hand stayed flat over her answers. She kept writing. Afterwards Mridul muttered, 'Some friend.'
Saturday. Nikita phoned him. 'I'm your friend. That's why I won't let you copy. If you get caught, it's both of us. Come over tomorrow; I'll go through the next chapter with you.' There was a long silence. Then, 'Okay. Bring the good pencils.'

qa.q: What did Mridul do in the test as a signal?
What was Nikita feeling during the test?
qa.a: Torn and embarrassed, her face burning, pulled between loyalty to Mridul and staying honest.

qa.q: What did Nikita offer instead of her answers?
qa.a: To go through the next chapter with Mridul at her home on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Mridul see Nikita's refusal at first?

grounding: Over three days a girl pressured by a friend to show answers feels torn, says no, and offers to help him study.

passage: 'Jeevan, your friend wants to copy your test? Your Lokesh Mama knows that feeling. In Class 6, my best friend Raghu leaned over during a science test and whispered, "Show me number four. We're friends, na? Friends help." My stomach twisted two ways. I loved Raghu. He had stood up for me against the big boys all year. But if the teacher saw, we'd both be in trouble, and he'd never actually learn it. I covered my paper and shook my head. He didn't speak to me for two days. On the third day I went to his house with my notebook and said, "I'll teach you four, five and six before the next test." He grumbled. But he passed. And we're still friends, fifty years on.'

qa.q: Which question did Raghu ask to see?
What was young Lokesh feeling when Raghu whispered?
qa.a: Torn, his stomach twisting two ways, between loyalty to Raghu and honesty.

qa.q: Which choice in the story kept both honesty and the friendship?
qa.a: Covering his paper, then going to Raghu's house to teach him before the next test.

qa.q: How might Raghu have felt during the two days of silence?
qa.a: Hurt and annoyed at being refused, and perhaps embarrassed too.

grounding: An uncle recalls a best friend using friendship to ask for answers, refusing, and offering to teach him instead.
